title: Generative AI at a glance
intro: Each chapter in a few visual slides: the mental model, the distinctions the questions turn on, and the concepts to practise next.

chapters.hook: What AI is, how machines learn, and how to tell whether a model is any good.

slides.title: AI, ML, deep learning, generative AI
slides.lede: Four terms, each a subset of the one before. The nesting is asked constantly and easy to invert under pressure.

layers.label: Generative AI
layers.sub: Deep learning that produces new content

layers.label: Deep learning
layers.sub: Machine learning with multi-layer neural networks

layers.label: Machine learning
layers.sub: Learns patterns from data instead of hand-written rules

layers.label: Artificial intelligence
layers.sub: Any technique that makes machines appear intelligent

points.t: Everything in production today is narrow AI — one defined task. General AI, with human breadth, does not exist.
Trained broadly at scale, then adapted to many downstream tasks.

slides.title: How machines learn
slides.lede: Learning paradigms differ in the signal the model learns from. Match the paradigm to the shape of the problem.

head: Paradigm
Learns from
Fits
rows: Labelled examples: input paired with the right answer
Labels derived from the data itself
Pretraining LLMs: predict the masked or next token

slides.title: Neural network basics
slides.lede: A neural network is layers of learned weights with non-linear functions between them.

items.label: Parameters
items.text: The weights and biases learned from data. “Model size” counts them.

items.label: Activation functions
items.text: Add non-linearity. Without them, any stack of layers collapses into one linear map.

items.label: Depth
items.text: More layers learn more abstract features, at the cost of harder training.

items.label: Convolution
items.text: For images: a small filter slides across the input, sharing weights across positions.

slides.title: Is the model any good?
slides.lede: The gap between training and validation performance tells you which problem you have.

cols.title: Overfitting
items: Stop early, at the validation minimum

points.t: At 97% negatives, always predicting “negative” scores 97%. Ask for precision, recall or the confusion matrix.
Tune on validation; touch the test set once, at the end.

slides.title: Framing an AI project
slides.lede: The most expensive mistakes happen before any model is trained.

slides.title: Responsible AI
slides.lede: A model learns whatever its data contains, including the unfairness. Responsibility is designed in, not added afterwards.

items.label: Bias from data
items.text: Historical data encodes historical decisions. The model reproduces them at scale.

items.label: Explainability
items.text: People affected by a decision should be able to understand why it was made.

items.label: Contestability
items.text: A route to challenge and correct a decision.

items.label: Transparency
items.text: Disclose when AI is used and what data it relies on.

items.label: AI and work
items.text: Automation changes tasks and roles; plan for the people affected.

slides.title: IBM watsonx
slides.lede: Three components, three jobs. The names give most of it away.

head: Component
Job
rows: Studio to train, validate, tune and deploy models, including foundation models
Lakehouse for storing and querying the data models use
Model risk documentation, drift monitoring, compliance and audit

chapters.hook: How generative models create, what they are good for, and why fluent is not the same as true.

slides.title: Four ways to generate
slides.lede: Generative models learn the distribution of their training data well enough to sample new examples from it. They differ in how.

items.label: GAN
items.text: A generator and a discriminator compete; the discriminator's judgement trains the generator.

items.label: VAE
items.text: Encodes inputs to a distribution over a latent space; sampling that space decodes to new data.

items.label: Diffusion
items.text: Learns to reverse a noising process, then denoises from pure noise, step by step.

items.label: Transformer
items.text: Attention over sequences, generating one token at a time. The basis of nearly every LLM.

points.t: A discriminative model learns to tell classes apart. A generative model learns what the data looks like, so it can produce more of it.

slides.title: How text gets generated
slides.lede: An LLM produces one token at a time. Each step is a probability distribution, and decoding decides which token to take.

nodes.label: Context
nodes.sub: The prompt plus tokens so far

nodes.label: Distribution
nodes.sub: A probability for every token in the vocabulary

nodes.label: Choose
nodes.sub: Sample, take the top token, or beam search

visual.loop: append the token and repeat — N tokens need about N forward passes

points.t: Low for extraction and structured output; higher for ideation and variety.
Keeps several candidate sequences and returns the most probable overall — common in translation.

slides.title: Fluent is not true
slides.lede: A language model is trained to produce plausible text, not true text. Hallucination is the default when it lacks the facts.

cols.title: Does not fix it
items: Asking the model to be accurate
Lowering temperature — that reduces variety, not invention

cols.title: Reduces it
items: “Answer only from the context, and say when it isn't there”
Verifying claims before acting on them

slides.title: Capabilities, limits and data
slides.lede: Use generative AI where plausible drafts are valuable and errors are cheap to catch.

points.t: A hosted provider may retain submitted data or use it for training. Check the terms before sending anything confidential or personal.

chapters.hook: Writing prompts that work reliably — and remembering they change nothing in the model.

slides.title: Anatomy of a prompt
slides.lede: A good prompt pins down six things. “Make it good” instructs nothing.

layers.label: Task
layers.sub: What to do, as a verb: summarise, classify, draft

layers.label: Context
layers.sub: The material and background it needs

layers.label: Format
layers.sub: Bullets, table, JSON, a single word

layers.label: Length
layers.sub: At most three sentences, under 200 words

points.t: More words do not help if they do not constrain the output.
“At most three sentences” beats “don't be verbose”.

slides.title: Prompting techniques
slides.lede: Each technique suits a different kind of task. The question usually describes the task.

head: Technique
Use when
rows: The task is common and the instruction alone carries it
The format or style is easier to show than to describe
The answer needs several reasoning steps
One correct answer exists; sample several chains and vote
The model should ask you questions before producing output
Tone and register need shaping — it confers no real expertise

slides.title: Self-consistency
slides.lede: One reasoning chain can go wrong at any step. Several independent chains rarely go wrong the same way.

points.t: Voting works for arithmetic and logic, not for open-ended writing.
Every extra chain is another full generation.

slides.title: Prompts in production
slides.lede: A prompt that ships is code: templated, versioned and tested.

items.label: Templates
items.text: Parameterised prompts with named variables, not strings pasted together.

items.label: Version and evaluate
items.text: Test every change on a fixed set of inputs, not on one output you happened to like.

items.label: Delimit untrusted text
items.text: Fence user and retrieved content. It marks the trust boundary against injection.

items.label: Examples teach everything
items.text: Few-shot examples teach whatever they share, intended or not. Vary what should vary.

slides.takeaway: Prompting changes nothing in the model — weights are fixed at inference. In-context learning lasts for one request, which is exactly why RAG works.

chapters.hook: Turning text into tensors, and the data and sizing decisions behind a model.

slides.title: From text to token ids
slides.lede: A model never sees text. It sees integer ids, and those ids only mean something relative to its own vocabulary.

points.t: An unseen word is composed from known fragments, and the vocabulary stays small.
The context window counts tokens, and covers the prompt and the output together.

slides.title: Tokenisers are not interchangeable
slides.lede: Each tool has a job. The model-specific tokenisers must match the model they were built for.

head: Tool
What it is for
rows: General linguistics: sentence and word segmentation, stemming, stop words
SentencePiece with XLNet's own vocabulary and special tokens

slides.takeaway: Always pair a model with its own tokeniser. Another vocabulary produces ids that mean something else entirely — and nothing raises an error.

slides.title: PyTorch data pipelines
slides.lede: Three pieces turn a corpus into batches. Each has one job.

nodes.label: collate_fn
nodes.sub: Pads a list of samples into one tensor

points.t: Padding to the dataset-wide maximum wastes compute on every batch.
Without the attention mask, outputs depend on what else is in the batch.

slides.title: Data quality beats scale
slides.lede: A model learns its training data's flaws as faithfully as its strengths. More bad data only teaches the flaws harder.

items.label: Diversity
items.text: Cover the topics, styles and languages the model will face.

items.label: Deduplication
items.text: Repeated text is over-weighted and memorised. Remove near-duplicates.

items.label: Quality filtering
items.text: Drop spam, boilerplate and broken text before training, not after.

items.label: Scale
items.text: Helps only once the data is clean. It cannot redeem bad data.

slides.title: Choosing a model size
slides.lede: The biggest model is rarely the right one. Choose the smallest that meets the quality bar within your constraints.

items.label: Latency
items.text: Larger models generate each token more slowly.

items.label: Memory
items.text: The weights must fit on the hardware you have, with room for the context.

items.label: Cost
items.text: Every request pays for the model's size.

items.label: Capability
items.text: Enough for the task — measured on your task, not a leaderboard.

chapters.hook: How words became vectors, how sequences were modelled before transformers, and how generated text is scored.

slides.title: From one-hot to contextual
slides.lede: Each step gives a word's representation more meaning and more context.

items.label: One-hot
items.sub: Every word equidistant from every other

items.label: Static embeddings
items.sub: word2vec, GloVe: one vector per word

slides.takeaway: Static embeddings give “bank” one vector whether it means a river bank or a savings bank. Contextual embeddings compute a different one each time.

slides.title: word2vec: two directions
slides.lede: Both variants learn embeddings by predicting words from their neighbours. They differ in which way the prediction runs.

cols.title: Skip-gram
items: Predict the surrounding words from the target

cols.title: CBOW
items: Predict the target from the surrounding words

slides.title: Sequence models before transformers
slides.lede: Each generation fixed the previous one's limit — until sequential computation itself became the limit.

head: Model
Idea
Limit
rows: Next word from the previous N−1
A hidden state carried across time
Gates keep a shorter gradient path
Still processes one step at a time
Encoder builds a representation; decoder generates from it
One fixed vector for the whole input

points.t: Training feeds the true previous token. At inference the model sees its own, which causes exposure bias.

slides.title: Scoring generated text
slides.lede: Automatic metrics are cheap and repeatable, and they measure surface overlap more than meaning.

items.label: Perplexity
items.text: How surprised the model is by held-out text. Lower is better; measures fit, not usefulness.

items.label: BLEU
items.text: N-gram precision against reference translations, with a brevity penalty.

items.label: ROUGE
items.text: Recall-oriented n-gram overlap, used for summarisation.

items.label: The catch
items.text: Overlap punishes valid paraphrases and rewards copied wording.

slides.title: Training mechanics
slides.lede: The same few controls decide whether a language model learns well.

items.label: Loss
items.text: Cross-entropy over the vocabulary: how much probability went to the right next token.

items.label: Learning-rate schedule
items.text: Warm up at the start, then decay. Too high diverges; too low stalls.

items.label: Underfitting
items.text: Training loss stays high: more capacity, more epochs, or check the data.

items.label: Overfitting
items.text: Validation loss rises while training loss falls: stop, regularise or add data.

chapters.hook: Attention, the transformer block, and why BERT and GPT are built differently.

slides.title: Attention in four steps
slides.lede: Each position asks a question of every other position, and takes a weighted mix of their answers.

nodes.label: Query · Key
nodes.sub: A relevance score for every pair of positions

nodes.label: Softmax
nodes.sub: Scores become weights that sum to 1

nodes.label: × Values
nodes.sub: A weighted average of the values

points.t: Several heads in parallel, in different subspaces, capture different kinds of relationship.
Self-attention looks within one sequence. Cross-attention lets the decoder query the encoder.
One score per pair of positions — cost grows with the square of sequence length.

slides.title: Inside a transformer block
slides.lede: A block moves information between positions, then transforms it within each position. Stacks repeat it many times.

layers.label: Token embeddings + positional encoding
layers.sub: Attention has no sense of order until this injects it

layers.label: Add & layer norm
layers.sub: Residual path around the sublayer; per-example normalisation

layers.label: Position-wise feed-forward
layers.sub: Transforms each position on its own

slides.title: Encoder, decoder, or both
slides.lede: BERT and GPT differ in masking and training objective — not in whether they use attention.

cols.title: Encoder
items: Sees the whole sequence in both directions

cols.title: Decoder
items: A causal mask hides later positions

slides.title: BERT pretraining
slides.lede: BERT learns from unlabelled text with two self-supervised tasks and a handful of special tokens.

head: Token
Role
rows: First position; its output represents the whole sequence
Separates segments and marks the end
Stands in for tokens to be predicted
Fills to batch length; excluded by the attention mask

points.t: About 15% of tokens are masked, and the model predicts them from context on both sides.
Does sentence B actually follow sentence A?

chapters.hook: Adapting a pretrained model: how much to change, and how to keep training on the rails.

slides.title: How much of the model to change
slides.lede: Start at the cheapest rung and climb only when it falls short.

items.label: LoRA
items.sub: Small low-rank updates; most of the gain

items.label: Full fine-tuning
items.sub: All weights; needs data and compute

points.t: Feature extraction trains fast and resists overfitting.
A pretrained head predicts the pretraining objective's outputs, not your labels.

slides.title: LoRA
slides.lede: Freeze the base model and learn the weight update as the product of two thin matrices.

items.label: the base model
items.text: Pretrained weights are never touched.

items.label: rank r
items.text: Two thin matrices; r sets capacity. Higher r adapts more and overfits small data sooner.

items.label: at serving time
items.text: Adapters are small, so many share one loaded base model.

items.label: 4-bit base
items.text: LoRA over a quantised base model, to fit in less memory.

slides.title: The Hugging Face workflow
slides.lede: From a one-line demo to a fine-tuned model, with a matched tokenizer and model throughout.

nodes.label: pipeline()
nodes.sub: Instant inference to try a task

slides.title: When fine-tuning goes wrong
slides.lede: Most fine-tuning failures have a standard cause and a standard fix.

rows: Smaller per-device batch; restore the effective batch with gradient accumulation
Learning rate too high — use roughly 1e-5 to 5e-5
General ability lost after narrow tuning
Catastrophic forgetting: mix general data back in, lower LR, fewer epochs
Different output on each evaluation run
Call model.eval() so dropout is off

chapters.hook: Teaching a model to follow instructions, then to prefer the answers people prefer.

slides.title: Instruction tuning
slides.lede: A pretrained model continues text. Training on many instruction–response pairs teaches it to follow instructions — including ones it never saw.

cols.title: Base model
items: Trained to predict the next token
A question may get more questions back

cols.title: Instruction-tuned
items: Supervised on instruction–response pairs across many tasks

slides.title: RLHF in three stages
slides.lede: Reinforcement learning from human feedback turns “which answer is better” into a training signal.

nodes.label: Supervised fine-tuning
nodes.sub: Demonstrations, so it responds sensibly at all

nodes.label: PPO
nodes.sub: Improve the policy against the reward

points.t: The model itself, seen as a distribution over next tokens: state is the context, action is the token.
Prompt, then SFT, then preferences — only when you can judge better or worse but cannot write the right answer.

slides.title: Reward models
slides.lede: A reward model scores responses so the scores agree with human preference. It never generates anything.

items.label: Pairwise, not absolute
items.text: “Which of these two is better?” is far less noisy than a 1–10 rating.

items.label: A scorer only
items.text: Takes a prompt and a response, returns one number.

items.label: Hold out preferences
items.text: Keep preference data the optimiser never sees, or rising reward is indistinguishable from memorisation.

items.label: Reward hacking
items.text: High score, useless output. Hedging and padding are the classic symptoms.

slides.title: PPO's safety catches
slides.lede: Optimising hard against a learned reward goes wrong fast. PPO adds two brakes.

cols.title: KL penalty
items: Penalises drifting from a frozen copy of the starting model
The reference is frozen so the anchor does not move

cols.title: Clipped objective
items: Caps how far one update can move the policy

slides.takeaway: PPO keeps the policy, the frozen reference and the reward model in memory at once. That cost is much of why DPO caught on.

slides.title: DPO: preferences without RL
slides.lede: Direct Preference Optimization reaches the same goal as RLHF with an ordinary supervised-style loss.

cols.title: RLHF with PPO
items: Policy, reference and reward model all resident

cols.title: DPO
items: No RL loop — trains directly on chosen vs rejected pairs

slides.takeaway: Why it works: DPO reparameterises the objective so the intractable partition function cancels in the ratio of chosen to rejected responses.

chapters.hook: Retrieval-augmented generation end to end, LangChain's building blocks, and when a chain becomes an agent.

slides.title: RAG: offline and per request
slides.lede: Half the work happens once, when documents are indexed. The other half happens on every question.
slides.takeaway: RAG for facts that change or answers that must cite sources; fine-tuning for stable behaviour and style. They solve different problems.

slides.title: Retrieval mechanics
slides.lede: Dense retrieval finds passages by meaning, using vectors and a fast nearest-neighbour index.

items.label: Dense passage retrieval
items.text: Separate question and passage encoders, trained so questions land near the passages that answer them.

items.label: FAISS
items.text: Fast nearest-neighbour search over dense vectors. It stores and searches — nothing more.

items.label: Top-k
items.text: Too few and the answer is missing; too many and the signal is diluted and the prompt costs more.

items.label: Always an answer
items.text: Similarity search returns its nearest neighbours however far away. Out-of-scope questions need a relevance threshold.

slides.title: Chunking
slides.lede: Chunk size decides whether one passage holds a whole answer.

cols.title: Too small
items: The answer is split across chunks

points.t: Content that crosses a boundary appears whole in at least one chunk.
Paragraphs and sections, not fixed character counts that cut sentences in half.

slides.title: Diagnose the RAG failure
slides.lede: Name the failing stage before changing anything.

rows: Topically right chunks that never contain the answer
Generation: context assembly, instructions, the model
Confident answer to an out-of-scope question
No relevance threshold or grading step
Its chunks are still in the index
New embedding model: re-embed the whole corpus

slides.title: LangChain's building blocks
slides.lede: Each component does one job. Questions often describe the job and ask for the component.

head: Component
Job
rows: Reads a source format into Documents with metadata
Picks which few-shot examples to include for this input
Turns model text into structured data
Query in, documents out — any backend
Composition: each step's output feeds the next
Chooses tools, observes results, decides what next

slides.title: Chain or agent?
slides.lede: The difference is who decides the next step: your code, or the model.

cols.title: Chain
items: Right when the steps are known

cols.title: Agent
items: Chooses tools and when to stop
More calls, more ways to fail

points.t: The model proposes a structured call; your code runs it and returns the result.
If the steps are known in advance, a chain is simpler and more reliable.

slides.title: Retrieved text is data
slides.lede: Anything retrieved or pasted in can contain instructions. The model cannot tell them apart from yours unless the structure does.

items.label: Injection through content
items.text: A document that says “ignore previous instructions” is read like any other text.

items.label: Fence it
items.text: Delimit retrieved and user text, and label it as data.

items.label: Keep privileges apart
items.text: Untrusted text never goes into the system or privileged section of the prompt.

items.label: Answer from context
items.text: Instruct the model to use only the context, and to say when the answer is not there.

chapters.hook: Assembling a working RAG application — integration decisions rather than new theory.

slides.title: The build, in order
slides.lede: The capstone wires components you already know. Getting the order and the contracts between them right is the work.

nodes.label: Embed & store
nodes.sub: One embedding model, one vector store

nodes.label: Gradio interface
nodes.sub: A front end over the chain

slides.takeaway: Embed the query with the same model that embedded the documents. Vectors from different models live in incomparable spaces.

slides.title: Citations and provenance
slides.lede: An answer the user cannot check is an answer they have to take on faith.

items.label: Carry the metadata
items.text: Source file, page or URL from the loader, kept with every chunk.

items.label: Return sources
items.text: Show which chunks the answer came from, alongside the answer.

items.label: Conflicting sources
items.text: Surface the conflict and cite both, rather than silently picking one.

slides.title: Keeping the index honest
slides.lede: The vector store is a copy of the corpus. It drifts out of date unless something keeps it in step.

items.label: Deletion
items.text: Removing a source file does nothing until its chunks are removed from the index.

items.label: Updates
items.text: Re-ingest changed documents and drop the chunks of their old versions.

items.label: Embedding changes
items.text: A new embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus.
